bib.title: Self-Organizing Agent Teams Learn to Reason Together

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Self-Organizing Agent Teams Learn to Reason Together", Pappu, Suzgun, Kwon, Bianchi, El, Kochenderfer, Cao, Zou (Stanford, Together AI, Emory). arXiv:2609.22682v1 [cs.AI], 19 Sep 2026. Preprint (no venue).

COVERAGE: Read the full 122,298-char extraction: main text, Tables 1-6, discussion/limitations, Appendix B, D, E, and the start/end of Appendix A (strategy banks) and Table 4. I read the middle of Appendix A (~65k-100k chars: strategy listings and transcripts, Figs 8-12) only by search. The reference list was skimmed. No scanned or garbled pages. Nothing in the text is an instruction to me.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Math/physics team beats best member, every compute control and the routing oracle on average.
 number: SAT 66.7% avg vs best member 48.8%, self-consistency K=10 55.4%, linearization 58.7%, Mixture of Agents 57.3%, debate 52.7%, routing oracle 59.0%.
 setup: o3-mini + Claude Sonnet 4 + DeepSeek-V3. Strategy bank learned on 15 AIME-2024 problems, frozen, run on held-out AIME24, AIME25, AIME26, HMMT Feb 2026 and TheoremQA-physics. Means over 3 seeds.
 quote: "the team averages 66.7% accuracy, compared with 48.8% for the best member, 57.3% for Mixture of Agents, 55.4% for self-consistency, and 58.7% for linearization (Table 1)."
 where: Sec. 4, p. 7; Table 1, p. 8.
2. On AIME 2026 the team exceeds a perfect router.
 number: SAT 71.2% vs oracle 57.8% (+13.4 pp); best member 42.2%; linearization 68.5%.
 setup: as above, transfer benchmark. The oracle is a per-problem selector over members' single independent answers.
 quote: "On AIME 2026, it reaches 71.2%, 29.0 percentage points above the best member and 13.4 percentage points above the routing oracle."
 where: p. 8.
3. The gain over the compute-matched single model is small or zero on some benchmarks.
 number: HMMT26 SAT 39.4 = linearization 39.4. Knowledge/logic average SAT 72.8 vs linearization 72.1.
 setup: linearization means the strongest member plays every role and phase serially. SAT leads on AIME25 (60.8 vs 43.3) and AIME26 (71.2 vs 68.5), and is lower on TQA-phys (77.2 vs 68.4, so higher; the math average gap is 8.0 pp).
 quote: "On the harder HMMT 2026, the team and matched linearization tie at 39.4%, compared with 26.3% for the best member." Also "SAT is best on GPQA but trails Mixture of Agents on MMLU-Pro (82.4% versus 84.3%)."
 where: p. 8; Table 2, p. 9.
4. Knowledge/logic team: best average, but below the routing oracle. Selecting the right answer is the bottleneck.
 number: SAT accuracy 72.8% vs oracle 79.6%; SAT pool coverage 87.9%; best member 65.9%; self-consistency 67.5%.
 setup: Gemini-2.5-Flash + Llama-4-Maverick + GPT-4.1. Bank learned on 25 GPQA Diamond problems. Evaluated on 100 held-out GPQA, 100 MMLU-Pro, 75 BBEH items (5 subtasks). BBEH: the homogeneous team leads at 58.7 and SAT is 56.0.
 quote: "its selected answers average 72.8% accuracy, below the oracle's 79.6% average coverage."
 where: p. 10; Table 2.
5. Heterogeneity matters. The same frozen strategies run by three copies of one model do much worse on math.
 number: homogeneous team (3x o3-mini) 56.0% vs SAT 66.7% on math. On knowledge/logic the gap is 70.9 vs 72.8.
 quote: "The homogeneous team averages 56.0% across the suite, indicating that the learned interaction structure successfully leverages model heterogeneity to improve performance."
 where: p. 7.
6. Demonstrability (can a judge panel tell correct from incorrect team reasoning) tracks SAT's gain over the best member.
 number: Spearman rho = 0.90, p = 0.005, n = 8 benchmarks. Leave-one-out rho 0.86-0.96.
 setup: ten small judge models (e.g. Gemma 3 4B, GPT-3.5 Turbo, Llama 3.1 8B) from outside both rosters. Each sees one correct and one wrong certificate in balanced A/B order. Demonstrability ranges from 0.423 (TQA-phys, +6.1 pp) to 0.687 (AIME26, +29.0 pp). Correlational and measured post hoc.
 quote: "Across eight benchmarks, demonstrability strongly tracks how much the self-organizing team improves over its strongest member (Spearman ρ= 0.90, p= 0.005)"
 where: abstract; Sec. 5, p. 11; Tables 5-6, p. 30.
7. The learned bank beats the unlearned starting protocol. Pinit is independent solves, 2 debate rounds, majority vote.
 number: math avg 54.1 vs 66.7. Knowledge/logic avg 69.6 vs 72.8.
 where: Table 4, App. B, p. 25.

IS COMPUTE MATCHED?
- Self-consistency K=10 matches the number of candidate solutions: "Self-consistency at K=10 matches the number of candidate solutions". It samples at temperature 0.5 from the best model for that benchmark.
- Five-pass self-reflection controls for single-agent reasoning depth.
- Linearization runs "at approximately the team's total inference budget". Self-consistency, self-reflection, linearization and the homogeneous team are flagged with a double-dagger as compute controls.
- No token counts, dollar costs or call counts are reported. Matching is by candidate count and "approximately" the budget, not by measured tokens. Mixture of Agents, debate and member-vote are not marked as compute controls.
- SAT cost is not stated. It runs the full bank of up to 10 strategies, each multi-phase, plus a judge call over all certificates. That is likely much more than 10 single samples.
- The single-agent baselines use the best model chosen per benchmark by single-pass accuracy. Self-consistency does not get the 3-model ensemble.
- Offline learning cost (6 mutation rounds per problem, up to 3 candidates per round, validation probes) is not counted in the comparison.

LIMITS
- Authors concede: richer generation does not guarantee correct selection (87.9% coverage vs 72.8% accuracy). Demonstrability is correlational and post hoc. Better selection or certificate formats are needed.
- Small test sets: 100 GPQA, 100 MMLU-Pro, 75 BBEH. AIME-type sets are about 30 problems per year, so single-problem swings are large. Only 3 seeds. No confidence intervals reported; I saw no significance tests apart from the Spearman.
- Models are deliberately mid-tier (o3-mini, Sonnet 4, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4.1, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Llama-4-Maverick). The authors chose them to "preserve headroom", so it is untested whether the gain holds with stronger models. These models are dated by late 2026.
- Only two 3-model rosters. Training sets are tiny (15 and 25 problems).
- The routing oracle is computed over one independent answer per member. It is not an oracle over 10 samples, so exceeding it is a weaker claim than beating best-of-K coverage. Self-consistency coverage is not reported.
- The linearization control can't separate multi-agent interaction from model heterogeneity (the authors say so).
- On math, the gap to linearization is 8.0 pp on average (66.7 vs 58.7), and 0.7 pp on knowledge/logic (72.8 vs 72.1).

BUILDS ON
- GEPA (Agrawal et al., ICLR 2026): reflective prompt evolution. SAT differs in that the designated member chooses the parent and mutation.
- Debate: Du et al., ICML 2024. Critiques of debate: Choi et al., NeurIPS 2025 (majority vote over initial answers explains most of debate's gain); Zhang et al., 2025a; Zhu et al., 2026.
- Mixture of Agents: Wang et al., 2025.
- Truth-wins and demonstrability: Lorge & Solomon 1955; Laughlin & Ellis 1986.
- Orchestration work: Conductor (Nielsen et al., ICLR 2026), OPTAGENT (Bi et al., 2025), GPTSwarm (Zhuge et al., 2024), AFlow, AgentNet, LATTE.
- Search: Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026), ADAS (Hu et al., ICLR 2025), Archon, DSPy (Khattab, ICLR 2024).
- Ensembles: Breiman 1996, Freund & Schapire 1997.

CODE: none. Appendix D.1 has the judge prompt: audit each certificate for "named_defects" without solving the problem, then pick the best-supported one, with a frequency tie-break among defect-free candidates (p. 29).

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p. 1): bars for best member, self-consistency, debate, MoA, SAT and routing oracle across 5 benchmarks, with +pp over the best member. It is the one figure candidate, since it shows the baseline set and the oracle in one view.
- Fig 6 (p. 11) is the demonstrability rank scatter.

PROBLEMS: The extraction of figure and table text is somewhat jumbled (Table 1 bold markers are lost, and Figure 4 is duplicated). The intro opens with a narrative about a July 2026 OpenAI incident (cited to OpenAI and METR posts). I did not verify it and it is not load-bearing.
